newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Africa campaign for top U.N. job hots up.
newsitem.headline: Africa campaign for top U.N. job hots up.

text.p: Africa's campaign for the top job at the U.N. intensified on Sunday with some presidents jostling to promote their favoured candidates and Nelson Mandela accusing France of planning to veto South Africa's choice.

Ghana, Ivory Coast, Niger and Mauritania have formally nominated nationals as candidates and other names were likely to follow before or after Monday, when the Security Council is expected to take an informal poll on levels of support.

Mandela told a Cape Town news conference on Sunday that Tanzania's Salim Ahmed Salim, secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity, was best placed to succeed Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali as U.N. secretary-general.
"He has done very well as secretary-general of the OAU," the South African president said. "We think he is the best candidate for the job."
Mandela said French President Jacques Chirac had threatened to veto Salim, who was in the West African Francophone state of Togo on Sunday for talks with President Gnassingbe Eyadema.

"I spoke at length last night to Jacques Chirac, who insists that a candidate for the secretary-generalship of the United Nations must be fluent in both English and French," Mandela added. "He said he will veto Salim Salim if he is nominated."

The OAU, which backed Boutros-Ghali at its annual summit in Cameroon in July, opened the door to other Africans when he temporarily stepped aside on Wednesday after a November 19 U.S. veto blocked his path to the traditional second term.

The United States says Boutros-Ghali, whose five-year term expires on December 31 and who reserves the right to rejoin the race, has not done enough to reform the United Nations but it has left the door open for other Africans.
Nominees so far declared are as follows:

-- Kofi Annan of Ghana, the U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping. He has held a variety of top-level U.N. posts and maintained a diplomatic silence while his boss Boutros-Ghali was still in the running.
-- Ahmedou Ould Abdallah of Mauritania, former U.N. special representative for Burundi and now a co-chairman of the Global Coalition for Africa group in Washington.
-- Hamid Algabid of Niger, the secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference.
-- Amara Essy of Ivory Coast. Ivorian foreign minister and the U.N. General Assembly president in 1994-95. He brokered a peace agreement ending five years of civil war in Sierre Leone.

Ghana President Jerry Rawlings, seeking a fresh mandate in national elections on Saturday, described Annan as an "extremely competent" person. "I hope my colleagues will consider his credentials when they are making their choice," he said.
Niger's Algabid never disguised his ambition even when African states were, in theory, united behind Boutros-Ghali. He circulated a colourful curriculum vitae at July's OAU summit.

Ivorian President Henri Konan Bedie says he expects Essy to win wide support plus the backing of former colonial ruler France, a permanent Security Council member. "Ivory Coast has only friends in the world. And we will present him so that he is accepted by all," he told state television.

Senegalese President Abdou Diouf backs his foreign minister, Moustapha Niasse, for the job. "I see in him the profile of a secretary-general of the United Nations and I have given my endorsement," he said on Friday.
But Senegal's ties with Taiwan make a Chinese veto likely.
